overlays.title: What is a Spiral Arm?
overlays.shortDescription: Density waves, not fixed groups of stars
overlays.fullDescription: Spiral arms are regions where stars, gas, and dust become temporarily compressed as they orbit the galaxy. They're not solid structures—stars enter and leave them as they move. The arms persist as density waves, similar to traffic jams on a highway.

overlays.title: What are Dust Lanes?
overlays.fullDescription: Dust lanes consist of microscopic particles (silicates, carbon, ice) that absorb and scatter light. They often mark the inner edges of spiral arms where material compresses, obscuring stars beyond them.

overlays.title: Why Does the Galaxy Have a Core?
overlays.fullDescription: During galaxy formation, gravitational collapse concentrates matter toward the center. This creates a dense bulge of old stars and often a supermassive black hole. The core's intense gravity anchors the entire galactic structure.

overlays.title: What is a Supermassive Black Hole?
overlays.shortDescription: Millions to billions of solar masses
overlays.fullDescription: Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) reside at galactic centers with masses from millions to billions of solar masses. They form through stellar collapse, black hole mergers, and direct gas accretion. SMBHs influence star formation and galactic evolution.

overlays.title: Where Do Stars Form?
overlays.shortDescription: Dense gas clouds in spiral arms
overlays.fullDescription: Stars form in molecular clouds where gas density and temperature allow gravitational collapse. Spiral arms compress gas, triggering star formation. Young, massive stars ionize surrounding gas, creating HII regions visible as nebulae.

overlays.title: What is Dark Matter?
overlays.fullDescription: Dark matter comprises ~85% of the universe's matter but doesn't emit, absorb, or reflect light. We detect it through gravitational effects. Galaxies are embedded in vast dark matter halos that provide the gravitational scaffolding for structure.

keyFact.unit: Dark matter to visible matter ratio

overlays.title: How Fast Does the Galaxy Rotate?
overlays.fullDescription: Galaxies don't rotate like solid bodies—inner regions orbit faster than outer regions (differential rotation). However, dark matter causes outer stars to move faster than expected based on visible mass alone, revealing dark matter halos.

overlays.title: Types of Nebulae
overlays.fullDescription: Emission nebulae glow from ionized gas (H-alpha red light). Reflection nebulae scatter blue starlight off dust. Dark nebulae are dense clouds that block background light. Each reveals different physical processes.
